lead: An image on a screen begins as light from a scene. A digital image stores that light only at finitely many grid points, each rounded to a finite set of values. Sampling chooses the points; quantisation chooses the values. The eye then rebuilds edges and contrast from this sparse data, often adding effects that are not in the pixels. This chapter explains how the grid, the number of levels and human vision together decide whether an image looks sharp, smooth or banded. It sits under every raster display, camera and image file.
prereq: You need: the raster grid idea from Chapter 1.2 and the RGB/HSV vocabulary from Chapter 1.4.

blocks.text: A continuous image gives a colour at every point (x, y). A digital image keeps values only on a rectangular grid. Each grid point is a sample; the stored value at that point is a pixel. Sampling is the choice of grid points. Quantisation is the rounding of each sample to a finite set of levels. A grey image with bit depth b stores integer levels from 0 to 2b − 1, where 0 is black and the maximum is white. An 8-bit grey image therefore has 0 to 255, or 256 levels. A colour image stores one level per channel, commonly red, green and blue.

blocks.where: N is the number of pixels; W is the width in pixels; H is the height in pixels.
N is the pixel count; C is the number of channels (1 for grey, 3 for RGB); b is the bit depth per channel; bytes is the uncompressed storage size.

blocks.text: Spatial resolution is the pixel count W × H. Bit depth controls how many levels each sample can take. The display reconstructs an image by spreading each sample over a small area; a larger pixel looks smoother but hides detail. A fine pattern that falls between samples can reappear as a false coarse pattern. This is aliasing.

ppi means pixels per inch: image pixels mapped to a physical inch. dpi means dots per inch: printer marks per inch. They are related but not the same. A 72 ppi file can be printed small and look sharp. Computer graphics creates samples from a geometric model; image processing changes samples that already exist. Both share the same grid, as Chapter 1.1 separates them.

sections.h3: Changing the grid: nearest and bilinear

blocks.text: Resizing asks for values between stored samples. Interpolation supplies them. Nearest-neighbour takes the closest sample. It is fast and keeps every original value, but edges become blocky when enlarged. Bilinear interpolation takes the four nearest samples and weights them by distance. For position (x, y) inside a cell, let a be the horizontal fraction and b the vertical fraction, both from 0 to 1. The four corners are I<sub>00</sub>, I<sub>10</sub>, I<sub>01</sub> and I<sub>11</sub>.
I(x, y) = (1 − a)(1 − b)I<sub>00</sub> + a(1 − b)I<sub>10</sub> + (1 − a)bI<sub>01</sub> + abI<sub>11</sub>
blocks.where: I(x,y) is the interpolated value; a and b are fractions across the cell; I00 is the top-left sample, I10 top-right, I01 bottom-left, I11 bottom-right.

blocks.text: Bilinear gives smooth ramps but softens edges. Averaging is a related operation: shrinking by two replaces each 2 × 2 block with its mean, as the figure shows. This lowers spatial resolution and cannot restore the lost detail.

The retina has two main receptor types. Rods are numerous, work in dim light and do not signal colour. Cones need more light, give colour and carry fine detail. Cones are concentrated in the fovea, so acuity, the ability to resolve fine detail, is highest at the centre of gaze and falls towards the periphery. A display can show a sharp centre and a soft edge and the eye will accept it if the centre is where attention lies.

Brightness is not judged linearly. The eye responds roughly logarithmically, so equal steps in stored grey value do not look equally spaced. Displays add a nonlinear transfer, called gamma, between code value and light. Without correction, mid-grey looks too dark or too bright.

Lateral inhibition in the retina sharpens edges. At a step from dark to light, the eye sees a dark band just before the step and a light band just after. These are Mach bands. Simultaneous contrast is the related effect where the same grey patch looks lighter on a black background than on a white one. The eye reports contrast and edges, not absolute pixel values. Anti-aliasing uses this: it softens a jagged edge with intermediate samples, and the eye reads a smoother line than the raw grid contains.

figure.caption: The worked example's scan pipeline: a 4 cm × 3 cm photo at 300 ppi becomes 472 × 354 = 167,088 pixels. Both files hold the same pixels; only the bytes per pixel change, so colour needs 489.5 KiB and grey needs 163.2 KiB.

spec.title: Worked example: 4 × 3 cm photo at 300 ppi
spec.aria: A flow chart: a 4 cm by 3 cm photo scanned at 300 ppi gives 472 by 354 pixels, which is 167,088 pixels in total; those pixels take 501,264 bytes as 24-bit colour (489.5 KiB) or 167,088 bytes as 8-bit grey (163.2 KiB).

examples.question: A passport photograph measures 4 cm by 3 cm. It is scanned at 300 ppi. Use 1 inch = 2.54 cm. Find the pixel width, pixel height, total pixel count, and uncompressed storage for 24-bit colour and 8-bit grey. Give bytes and KiB, with 1 KiB = 1024 bytes. Round each pixel dimension to the nearest whole pixel.
steps: Width in pixels = 1.574803 × 300 = 472.4409, nearest whole pixel = 472.
Height in pixels = 1.181102 × 300 = 354.3307, nearest whole pixel = 354.
24-bit colour uses 3 bytes per pixel because 24 ÷ 8 = 3 bytes. Storage = 167,088 × 3 = 501,264 bytes.
8-bit grey uses 1 byte per pixel. Storage = 167,088 × 1 = 167,088 bytes.
examples.answer: Pixel size is 472 × 354, total 167,088 pixels; 24-bit colour needs 501,264 bytes (489.5 KiB) and 8-bit grey needs 167,088 bytes (163.2 KiB).
examples.check:
w_cm = 4
h_cm = 3
ppi = 300
cm_per_in = 2.54
w_in = w_cm / cm_per_in
w_px = round(w_in * ppi)
h_in = h_cm / cm_per_in
h_px = round(h_in * ppi)
total = w_px * h_px
color_bytes = total * 3
grey_bytes = total * 1
print(w_px)
print(h_px)
print(total)
print(color_bytes)
print(round(color_bytes / 1024, 1))
print(grey_bytes)
print(round(grey_bytes / 1024, 1))

traps: Pixel count is not physical size. A 72 ppi image can be printed small and sharp; the same file printed large looks soft. ppi belongs to the file-to-device mapping, not to the pixel array alone.
ppi and dpi are not the same. ppi counts image pixels per inch; dpi counts printer ink dots per inch, and one pixel may need several dots.
24-bit colour is 8 bits per channel, not 24 bits per channel. Storage uses 3 bytes per pixel, not 24 bytes.
Equal steps in stored grey value are not equal steps in perceived brightness; the eye is roughly logarithmic and displays add gamma.
Aliasing is not blur. Blur removes high frequencies; aliasing folds them to false low frequencies.

quiz.a: Sampling chooses the grid points where a continuous image is measured. Quantisation rounds each measurement to a finite set of levels. A pixel is the stored sample at one grid point.

quiz.q: A fine checkerboard is sampled too coarsely and shows a coarse false pattern. Name the effect and explain the cause.
quiz.a: The effect is aliasing. Fine detail above half the sampling rate is folded to a lower spatial frequency, so the eye sees a false coarse pattern instead of the original detail.

quiz.q: A 200 × 150 RGB image uses 8 bits per channel. Find its uncompressed storage in bytes and KiB, with 1 KiB = 1024 bytes.
quiz.a: Pixels = 200 × 150 = 30,000. RGB uses 3 bytes per pixel, so storage = 30,000 × 3 = 90,000 bytes. In KiB, 90,000 ÷ 1024 = 87.890625 ≈ 87.9 KiB.

quiz.q: A grey square looks lighter on a black background than on a white background. Name the effect and explain the retinal cause.
quiz.a: This is simultaneous contrast. Retinal lateral inhibition compares each patch with its surround. A dark surround gives less inhibition, so the same grey signal is perceived as lighter.

quiz.q: Compare nearest-neighbour and bilinear interpolation for enlarging an image.
quiz.a: Nearest-neighbour copies the closest sample: fast, preserves original values, but gives blocky edges. Bilinear weights four neighbouring samples by distance: smoother, but softens edges and creates new values.

quiz.q: How many grey levels does a bit depth of 6 give?
Why do Mach bands appear near a sharp brightness step, and why does anti-aliasing make a jagged line look smoother?
quiz.a: Mach bands come from lateral inhibition: the retina overshoots near an edge, producing a dark band on the dark side and a light band on the light side. Anti-aliasing replaces a hard jagged step with intermediate samples; the eye averages them and reads a smoother edge than the pixel grid alone would suggest.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production cameras add demosaicing, noise reduction and tone mapping before a file exists. Display systems apply gamma and colour management so code values produce intended light. Research in perceptual metrics predicts visible error using contrast sensitivity instead of raw pixel differences. Search terms: modulation transfer function, contrast sensitivity function, gamma correction, demosaicing.
